title: What the venue owner adds to our keyword research

content.job: Standalone list email exploring the central exchange and the roles on each side. Preserve the body exactly. No offer or reply request; send metadata remains proposed.
content.body:
Our team had brought the existing keywords and some proposed additions to the conversation. She explained that the shortened name was familiar to local people, as well as some couples coming from outside the area. If couples use a name like that when they talk about the area, some may use it when they search, and a keyword list put together from outside the market can miss a term like that.

The team agreed to look into her suggestion and share any additional terms they found.

It was a small exchange, but it illustrates something we value in an advertising partnership. Our team contributed the recommendations and the commitment to research. The client contributed context about how people talk about her market.

**Your firsthand knowledge of couples deserves a place alongside our advertising expertise.**

When you're already investing in Google Ads, you want the people supporting you to bring considered recommendations. You also have knowledge gained through the conversations you're having with people who might choose your venue.

Those contributions can work together. The person speaking with couples can offer context that's useful to the team researching how to reach them.

We believe a recommendation should give us something meaningful to discuss with you. There should be room for your experience to contribute while we're considering the strategy, with our team taking responsibility for investigating the questions that arise.

That's what this client brought to the review. She explained a familiar way of referring to the region, and our team gave that suggestion a place in the research conversation.
content.ending:
If you advertise your venue, the way your couples talk about it can be useful in a conversation about your Google Ads, just as this client's suggestion gave our team something to look into.

Talk soon,
Whitney

content.title: What you hear from couples belongs in your Google Ads strategy.

slides.job: State the promise as an insight about the reader.
slides.text:
What you hear from couples belongs in your Google Ads strategy.

You can hire specialists for their advertising expertise and still bring valuable knowledge to the work. The way couples describe your area is part of what you know from speaking with them, and it's worth bringing along when your keywords are researched.

slides.job: Establish the prepared recommendations and the invitation.
slides.text:
In a review with a venue client, we brought the current Google keywords and some recommended additions into the discussion.

Then we asked what questions she had about the terms. That gave her a place to contribute her understanding of the market while the recommendations were still being considered.

slides.job: Keep the client's contribution and conditional reasoning exactly as approved.
slides.text:
She raised the shortened name people use for the region.

She explained that it was familiar to local people and to some couples coming from outside the area. The suggestion came from her knowledge of how people refer to the place where the venue operates. If couples use that name in conversation, some may use it when they search, and a keyword list put together from outside the market can miss it.

slides.job: Resolve the exchange with the evidenced research commitment.
slides.text:
We said we'd research it and pass along anything else we turned up.

She supplied the local context, and we took responsibility for investigating it. Her idea joined the recommendations we'd already prepared as something we had committed to explore.

slides.job: Connect the story to an owner who already speaks with couples.
slides.text:
If you're already advertising your venue, you have something useful to bring to this kind of partnership.

You're speaking with people who are considering getting married in your area. You hear how they describe the location and how familiar it is to them. That perspective can feed the work your advertising team is doing.

slides.job: Explain why an observation need not be a finished advertising recommendation.
slides.text:
Her suggestion didn't need to be a finished keyword.

She explained a name she knew and why it might be worth a look. That added another question to a review that already had prepared recommendations.

slides.job: State the partnership belief with a clear division of work.
slides.text:
**She shared what she knew about her market, and the research stayed with our team.**

You can contribute context from your market. We can investigate what it means for the advertising recommendations.

slides.job: Pay off the promise through the team's specific response.
slides.text:
So here's what working with us can look like.

You don't need to arrive with a finished keyword. A detail you've picked up from couples is enough to start with. For this client, our team agreed to look into her suggestion and share any additional terms we found.

slides.job: Close for both management and guided-launch readers without an explicit ask.
slides.text:
Whether you want a team to manage your ads or to launch your campaigns and guide you while you run them, your knowledge of couples still belongs in the partnership.

In this review, our recommendations and her knowledge of the area both had a place in the conversation.

caption.body:
You already market your venue, and you speak with the couples considering it every week. You want specialists running your search ads, and you also want them to make use of what you've learned from those conversations.

A keyword discussion with a venue client gives a small example. We reviewed the terms already in place and our proposed additions, then invited her perspective. She raised the abbreviation people use for the region and described its familiarity among locals and some couples visiting from elsewhere.

We agreed to investigate and report back with any further terms we found. The client contributed the context; our team committed to the research.

A prepared recommendation gave us something to discuss, and the client's explanation supplied another possibility to examine. Neither had to replace the other.

For someone who already knows the market, specialist support can give that experience a practical way to inform what gets considered next, without handing them the research.

caption.ending: Her suggestion had a defined next step, with our team responsible for looking into it.

content.script:
A venue client gave our team another phrase to investigate for her Google Ads.

Here's what happened. Our team was reviewing the keywords she already had, along with some additional recommendations. And they asked whether she had any questions or concerns about the list.

She brought up the shorthand people use for her area. She explained that local people use it, and some couples from outside the area do, too. If couples use a name like that when they talk about the area, some of them may use it when they search. A keyword list put together from outside the market can miss a term like that.

Our team said they'd look into it and share any other terms they found.

What stands out to me is how she contributed. She brought something she knew about the way people talk about her market into the research conversation.

When you're speaking with couples, you're hearing language that can be useful to the people working on your ads. We bring our advertising expertise, and you bring that firsthand experience.

I think a good partnership should give both a place in the strategy, so your knowledge of couples can help shape what our team explores.

content.job: Answers a question venue owners ask about who their Google Ads should reach, through the recommendation our team gave a venue client and the reasoning behind it.
beats: Open on the owner's own question: should Google Ads reach only women if most inquiries come from women?
Backstory: the form mentioned women, our team double-checked, she said some men inquire and asked whether to focus on one or both.
Our recommendation: include both and bid a little higher for women rather than excluding men, as a way to start; she said it sounded good.

content.title: Reel 2: include men or target women only on Google
content.script:
Should your Google Ads only reach women if most of your inquiries come from women? A venue client asked us that.

A little backstory. Her form had mentioned women and not men, so our team double-checked that she still wanted to target women only. She said she does get some men inquiring, though definitely more women, and she asked whether it's better to focus on one or try to attract both.

I explained that a lot of the time, we include both. Instead of excluding men, we can let Google know we're okay bidding a little higher for women, paying a bit more per lead, since that's who most of her inquiries come from. I said that could be a good way to approach it at the start, and she said that sounded good to her.

One of our strategists added some context, too. On Meta, being specific about who you reach matters a little more. On the Google side, we can be more flexible.

What I like about this one is that her question had a real answer that wasn't a simple yes or no. She knows who reaches out to her. We know how to reflect that in the way Google bids, and still reach the men who are searching too.

That's the kind of question we love working through with our clients.

The Google keywords this venue already had gave our team something useful to work with.

caption.body:
When you've invested time in an account, you want the next recommendation to reflect an understanding of what is already there. That includes recognising useful choices, as well as finding opportunities to develop the campaign.

In this venue's review, our team began by noting the keywords the venue already had in place. The ads were running before this conversation, and the team considered the existing terms good.

The discussion then covered that list together with proposed additions. The recommendations were presented in relation to the current account, giving the client a view of both the established terms and the further possibilities being considered.

That is a useful part of specialist support for a business already advertising. Previous work provides context for the next decision, and a positive assessment can be part of the review rather than something passed over.

We want our recommendations to reflect an understanding of the work already in place, so the client can see how the proposed changes relate to what has come before.

content.title: Reel 3: all-inclusive searches in the proposed keywords

caption.body:
When your venue offers something specific, you want your Google Ads to reflect it, not just your location. Couples can search for a place to get married while also saying exactly how they want the day put together.

During this Google review, our team saw the venue's all-inclusive offering as something that really sets it apart, and an opportunity to reflect it in the proposed searches. The suggestions included language about both all-inclusive venues and all-inclusive wedding packages.

The rationale came from a real part of the business: this was an option the venue offered, and someone intentionally searching for it could be looking for that kind of wedding arrangement.

Our team also discussed search volume, cost and competition for those terms. Those considerations came with the recommendations, so the client had more than a list of possible phrases to review, and she was asked for any questions or objections.

For a venue investing in specialist support, that explanation matters. Here, the proposed all-inclusive searches tied back to an option this venue actually offers, and the search volume, cost and competition behind them were part of the conversation.

Email: replaced the first-person reflection in the ending with a plain statement of how we handle what owners share, keeping no explicit ask.

Reel 1: script and caption body kept as locked; on-screen hook set to the plan's opening and the brief's hook moved to the cover so cover and hook differ; caption ending rewritten to avoid a personal reflection in a caption.

Reel 2: replaced the existing-keywords premise with the plan's targeting premise and wrote a new face-to-camera script and caption from the 19:34 to 20:57 turns in reported speech, leaving out budget and the client's estimate.

Reel 3: kept the locked hook and first screen; rewrote screens 2 and 3 for clarity with the sound off; caption adds the reader's desire and the strategist's view that the all-inclusive offer sets the venue apart.

Carousel: slide 3 kept as locked; slides 1, 2 and 4 reworded to remove spans shared with the email and Reel 1; slide 8 rewritten so it pays off the promise instead of repeating slide 4; caption tightened with the reader's situation.
